record_type_quote: In this preregistered experiment, we aimed to address five limitations of prior research on the effects of alcohol on moral judgment: (a) relatively low (or inconsistent) levels of alcohol consumption, (b) lack of a placebo condition in some studies, (c) small sample sizes, (d) confounds in the measurement of moral dilemma judgments, and (e) generalization to utilitarian judgments writ large based on responses to sacrificial dilemmas.

targets.title: The drunk utilitarian: Blood alcohol concentration predicts utilitarian responses in moral dilemmas.
targets.evidence_quote: First, because Duke and Bègue’s (2015) study used a correlational design, the obtained relations between blood alcohol concentration and moral judgment may not necessarily reflect a causal effect of alcohol.
targets.outcome_quote: Together, these results pose a challenge to the “drunk utilitarian” phenomenon and raise important questions about how alcohol may influence moral judgments, if it has any such effect at all.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The null effect contradicts the original positive association.

targets.authors: Arutyunova, K. R., Bakhchina, A. V., Krylov, A. K., & Alexandrov Yu, I.
targets.title: The effects of alcohol on heart rate and evaluation of actions in moral dilemma.
targets.evidence_quote: Subsequent laboratory experiments (Arutyunova et al., 2017; Francis et al., 2019) aimed to address this concern, and these studies did not find any significant effects of alcohol on moral judgments. However, the consumed doses of alcohol were relatively small in these experiments.
targets.outcome_quote: Despite these improvements, we failed to obtain any significant effect of alcohol on moral judgments.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The paper retests the prior experimental null effect with a higher dose and larger sample; its null result agrees.
